title: Common monomial denominators for finite supports
statement: Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $G$ an abelian group, and $Q\subseteq G$ a submonoid whose generated subgroup is $G$. Use the additive monoid conventions of [def-trf-fine-fan-blowup]. For $M=Q,G$, write $R[M]=\bigoplus_{m\in M}Re^m$ with $e^me^n=e^{m+n}$, and let $\iota:R[Q]\to R[G]$ send $e^q$ to $e^q$. Every $g\in G$ has a representation $g=a-b$ with $a,b\in Q$, and then $e^g e^b=e^a$ in $R[G]$. For every finite $T\subseteq G$ there exists $b\in Q$ with $b+T\subseteq Q$. More precisely, for any choices $g=a_g-b_g$ with $a_g,b_g\in Q$ for $g\in T$, the element $b=\sum_{g\in T}b_g$ has $b+g=a_g+\sum_{t\in T\setminus\{g\}}b_t\in Q$ for every $g\in T$. For $F=\sum_{g\in T}c_ge^g\in R[G]$, with $c_g\in R$, put $f=\sum_{g\in T}c_ge^{a_g+\sum_{t\in T\setminus\{g\}}b_t}\in R[Q]$. Then $\iota(f)=e^bF$. These formulas include $T=\varnothing$, with $b=0$ and $f=0$. The element $e^b$ is a unit of $R[G]$ with inverse $e^{-b}$.

source.place: ILO VIII 3.2.4, printed p.103, and Lemma 3.2.9 proof, printed p.104: the common dense group-algebra torus; explicit group-difference and finite-support denominators, old item steps 4–5.

proof.text: Use the additive convention of [def-trf-fine-fan-blowup]. Put $D=\{a-b:a,b\in Q\}\subseteq G$. It contains $0=0-0$ and $Q$ since $q=q-0$. Moreover $(a-b)+(c-d)=(a+c)-(b+d)$ and $-(a-b)=b-a$, so $D$ is a subgroup. Since the subgroup generated by $Q$ is $G$, it is contained in $D$, hence $D=G$. This gives $g=a-b$ for every $g\in G$; the defining multiplication of monomials gives $e^g e^b=e^{g+b}=e^a$.

source.place: VIII 3.2.4, printed p.103; elementary expansion of the group-completion input to the common torus.

proof.text: For finite $T\subseteq G$, choose $g=a_g-b_g$ as in step 1 for each $g\in T$, and put $b=\sum_{t\in T}b_t\in Q$. For $g\in T$, separate the $g$-summand and use commutativity in $G$: $b+g=b_g+\sum_{t\in T\setminus\{g\}}b_t+(a_g-b_g)=a_g+\sum_{t\in T\setminus\{g\}}b_t$. Every summand on the right belongs to $Q$, so the right side belongs to $Q$. This proves $b+T\subseteq Q$ and proves the displayed formula for any prescribed representations, not merely the ones just chosen.

source.place: VIII 3.2.4 and Lemma 3.2.9 proof, printed pp.103–104; explicit finite-denominator calculation for the common group algebra.

proof.text: For the prescribed coefficients, all exponents $a_g+\sum_{t\in T\setminus\{g\}}b_t$ belong to $Q$ by step 2, so the stated finite sum defines $f\in R[Q]$. The map $\iota$ preserves coefficients and sends each basis monomial to the monomial with the same exponent in $G$. Thus finite distributivity and step 2 give $\iota(f)=\sum_{g\in T}c_ge^{b+g}=\sum_{g\in T}e^b(c_ge^g)=e^b\sum_{g\in T}c_ge^g=e^bF$. This uses exactly the monomial multiplication and finite-sum definition of the algebras in the statement.

source.place: VIII 3.2.4 and Lemma 3.2.9 proof, printed pp.103–104; elementary expansion in the monomial basis.

proof.text: If $T=\varnothing$, the sum defining $b$ is $0\in Q$, and both $F$ and $f$ are empty sums, hence $0$; the containment is vacuous and $\iota(f)=e^0\,0=0$. For every $b\in Q$, both $e^b$ and $e^{-b}$ lie in $R[G]$, and $e^be^{-b}=e^{b-b}=e^0=1=e^{-b}e^b$. Consequently $e^b$ is a unit with the claimed inverse, including in the zero ring.

source.place: VIII 3.2.4, printed p.103; empty-family case and explicit inverse in the group algebra.
